title: LMFIT: Non-Linear Least-Square Minimization and Curve-Fitting for Python
abstract: Lmfit provides a high-level interface to non-linear optimization and curve fitting problems for Python. Lmfit builds on Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm of scipy.optimize.leastsq(), but also supports most of the optimization method from scipy.optimize. It has a number of useful enhancements, including: Using Parameter objects instead of plain floats as variables. A Parameter has a value that can be varied in the fit, fixed, have upper and/or lower bounds. It can even have a value that is constrained by an algebraic expression of other Parameter values. Ease of changing fitting algorithms. Once a fitting model is set up, one can change the fitting algorithm without changing the objective function. Improved estimation of confidence intervals. While scipy.optimize.leastsq() will automatically calculate uncertainties and correlations from the covariance matrix, lmfit also has functions to explicitly explore parameter space to determine confidence levels even for the most difficult cases. Improved curve-fitting with the Model class. This which extends the capabilities of scipy.optimize.curve_fit(), allowing you to turn a function that models for your data into a python class that helps you parametrize and fit data with that model. Many pre-built models for common lineshapes are included and ready to use. The lmfit package is Free software, using an MIT license

narrative:
Short impact summary

LMFIT has developed into a widely used software method anchor for Python-based non-linear least-squares fitting. The record shows substantial scholarly uptake: 1,324 citations, 1,349 documented downstream reuses, and 4,026 downloads, indicating that it is not only being cited but actively used in research workflows.

Full narrative

Published in 2014 and released openly through Zenodo, LMFIT provides a high-level interface for non-linear optimization and curve fitting in Python. Its design builds on established SciPy methods while adding parameter objects, bounds, and constraints that make model fitting more flexible in practice. That combination appears to have supported durable adoption across scientific communities.

The citation record is broad and sustained. OpenAlex lists 1,324 citations, with growth continuing across successive years, and the citing literature is concentrated in high-visibility venues such as The Astrophysical Journal, Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, Astronomy and Astrophysics, bioRxiv, and The Astronomical Journal. This pattern suggests that LMFIT has become a routine methodological component in research areas that rely on quantitative model fitting.

The downstream reuse evidence is similarly strong. The work is documented as reused by a wide mix of articles, preprints, conference papers, dissertations, software papers, and other scholarly outputs, which is consistent with a tool that functions as infrastructure rather than a one-off method description. Scite also records two supporting citation statements, reinforcing the picture of positive methodological uptake in the literature.

Usage metrics point in the same direction: the Zenodo record has drawn 54,664 views and 4,026 downloads. Taken together with the citation and reuse patterns, the evidence shows a mature and widely embedded software tool with sustained relevance in scholarly computing, especially in astronomy and related quantitative fields. Public-discourse and event-data signals are unavailable in this record, so the strongest evidence here comes from scholarly citations, reuse, and repository usage.
